note: Places to watch sport, places to play it, and places to run. Evergreen — fixtures change weekly, so cards link to the club's own ticketing rather than pretending to know who is at home in three weeks. Dated fixtures and races live in events.json so they expire on their own.

items.title: Paris FC at Stade Jean-Bouin
items.area: Stade Jean-Bouin, 20 avenue du Général Sarrail
items.transit: M9 to Porte de Saint-Cloud
items.times: Ligue 1, roughly every other weekend, August to May
items.why: The smart way to watch top-flight football in Paris. Paris FC came back up to Ligue 1 after forty-six years away, they play in a 20,000-seat stadium rather than a 48,000-seat one, and you can actually buy a ticket the week of the match at a sane price. PSG is the famous answer; this is the one you will get into.

pairings.text: Pre-match beer on rue du Commandant Guilbaud
Bois de Boulogne, 15 min west

items.title: PSG at the Parc des Princes
items.area: Parc des Princes, 24 rue du Commandant Guilbaud
items.transit: M9 to Porte de Saint-Cloud
items.times: Over twenty home matches through to the end of May
items.why: The big one, and worth doing once for the noise from the Auteuil end alone. Two warnings: league tickets sell out to members long before general sale, and resale prices are absurd. Aim for a midweek league fixture against a small club rather than a Champions League night — same stadium, same atmosphere, a third of the price. The stadium tour is a decent consolation if the fixtures do not work.

pairings.text: Bars around Porte de Saint-Cloud fill 2h before
Parc des Princes to the Bois is a 20-min walk

items.title: Red Star at Stade Bauer
items.area: Stade Bauer, Saint-Ouen
items.transit: M13 to Garibaldi, or M14 to Saint-Ouen
items.times: Home matches most other weekends in the season
items.why: Founded in 1897 by the man who also founded FIFA, and the most loved small club in France — anti-fascist terrace culture, brass bands, hand-painted banners, and a ground squeezed between houses that has just been rebuilt. Tickets are about a tenner and nobody checks whether you know the offside rule. Combine it with the Saint-Ouen flea market in the morning; they are ten minutes apart.

pairings.text: Puces de Saint-Ouen in the morning — 10 min away
Marché Paul Bert has wine bars in the aisles

items.title: Stade de France
items.area: Saint-Denis
items.priceNote: From ~€30 for rugby, more for France football
items.transit: RER B to La Plaine–Stade de France, or RER D to Stade de France–Saint-Denis
items.why: Eighty thousand seats, and both the RER B and the RER D stop at the door. France football and rugby internationals, the Top 14 final in June, and the Six Nations in February and March, which is the one to aim for — the singing before a France–Ireland match is worth the ticket on its own. Book Six Nations months ahead.

pairings.text: The Olympic Aquatics Centre is directly opposite
Two stops back into central Paris after

items.title: Paris Basketball at the Adidas Arena
items.area: Adidas Arena, Porte de la Chapelle
items.transit: M12 to Porte de la Chapelle
items.times: EuroLeague and French league nights, autumn to spring
items.why: Paris's newest arena, built for the 2024 Games and now the home of a EuroLeague basketball club that did not exist ten years ago. Eight thousand seats, so you are close to the floor wherever you sit. Basketball is the easiest live sport to walk into cold — the rules are obvious and the tickets are cheap.

pairings.text: Skatepark under the arena, free
Tamil quarter is 10 min east

items.title: Accor Arena, Bercy
items.area: 8 boulevard de Bercy
items.transit: M5 or M14 to Bercy
items.why: The sloping grass-sided pyramid by the river, on line 5 and line 14. Worth watching the calendar for two things in particular: the Paris Grand Slam judo in February, which is the best-attended judo event on earth, and the NBA Paris Games in January. Handball and gymnastics fill the gaps.

pairings.text: Parc de Bercy next door
Bercy Village for a drink after

items.title: Roland-Garros
items.area: 2 avenue Gordon Bennett, Porte d'Auteuil
items.transit: M10 to Porte d'Auteuil
items.times: Main draw late May to early June · grounds and museum year round
items.why: The insider move is qualifying week, the week before the tournament proper: tickets are a fraction of the price, sold without a ballot, and you can stand two metres from players who will be in the top twenty within a year. The main draw runs a public ballot the previous winter — put your name in around December. Outside the season the grounds and the tennis museum are open, and Court Philippe-Chatrier is genuinely impressive empty.

pairings.text: Serres d’Auteuil glasshouses, next door and free
Coffee in Auteuil village before the gates open

items.title: Night Racing at Vincennes
items.area: Hippodrome de Paris-Vincennes
items.transit: RER A to Joinville-le-Pont, then a short walk
items.times: Floodlit trotting meetings on winter evenings
items.why: Harness racing under floodlights on a winter night, for the price of a coffee, with a crowd of serious old men studying form sheets and almost no visitors at all. The Prix d'Amérique in late January is the biggest trotting race in the world. You do not need to bet, though a two-euro flutter makes it much more fun.

pairings.text: Bois de Vincennes before the floodlights come on
Dinner back at Nation

items.title: The Olympic Aquatics Centre
items.area: Saint-Denis, opposite the Stade de France
items.transit: RER B or D to Stade de France, then about ten minutes on foot
items.times: Open to the public daily — check session times
items.why: The only permanent venue built for the 2024 Games, and since summer 2025 you can just turn up and swim in it. Two fifty-metre pools, one of them open-air, plus the diving pool, a spa, padel courts, five-a-side, three-on-three basketball and a skatepark. It costs about the same as an ordinary municipal pool. This is the single most underused thing in this whole guide.

pairings.text: Stade de France is across the footbridge
Bakeries on rue de la République, Saint-Denis

items.title: Swimming in the Seine
items.area: Bras Marie (4th), Bercy (12th), Grenelle (15th)
items.transit: M7 to Pont Marie for the closest site
items.times: Summer only, roughly July to end of August, lifeguarded hours
items.why: They cleaned the river and reopened it to swimmers after a hundred-year ban, and hardly anyone has quite absorbed that this is now possible. Three supervised sites, free, with changing rooms and lifeguards. Bras Marie by Île Saint-Louis is the closest to you. Water quality is tested daily and sites shut after heavy rain, so check before you set off — but on a hot August afternoon there is nothing else like it.

pairings.text: Berthillon on Île Saint-Louis, 5 min
Square Barye at the island’s tip

items.title: Piscine Pontoise
items.area: 19 rue de Pontoise
items.transit: M10 to Maubert–Mutualité
items.times: Late-night swims until around 23:45 on some weekdays
items.why: A 1933 art deco pool with two tiers of little wooden changing cabins around a blue-tiled hall, and a glass roof. Krzysztof Kieślowski filmed here. The reason to know about it is the late session: swimming lengths at eleven at night under that roof, with almost nobody else in the water, is a genuinely strange and lovely thing to do on a weekday.

pairings.text: Late drink on rue Mouffetard
Circus Bakery cinnamon buns in the morning

items.title: Bouldering at Arkose
items.area: Several gyms — Nation, Montreuil, Massy
items.transit: M9 to Nation for the closest
items.why: Bouldering is the easiest way into climbing — no ropes, no partner, no technique required on your first visit, just problems a few metres off a thick mat. Arkose builds its gyms into old industrial buildings with a bar and a canteen attached, so it works as an evening out rather than a training session. Very good as a pair: you take turns and talk each other up things.

pairings.text: Arkose has its own canteen and bar
Paname Art Café for comedy after

items.title: Book a Municipal Tennis Court
items.area: Around forty sites across the city
items.transit: Nearest to you: Jules Ladoumègue and Alfred Nakache
items.why: The city runs about forty tennis centres and anyone can book one online for roughly the price of two coffees an hour. Almost no one who moves to Paris realises this and instead assumes tennis means a private club. Create a Paris account, book seven days ahead, and off-peak weekday courts are usually wide open.

pairings.text: Coffee wherever you booked — every centre has one nearby
Most municipal courts sit inside a park

items.title: The Canal Run
items.area: Canal Saint-Martin, then up the Ourcq
items.why: The flattest, straightest, most car-free run in Paris. Start where the Canal Saint-Martin comes out of the ground at République and follow the water north — out and back to the Bassin de la Villette is about 6 km; carry on up the Ourcq towards Pantin and you can make it 15 km without crossing a single road. Best before eight, when it is just runners and the lock keepers.

stops.text: Start on the canal at Jemmapes
North past the locks and the iron footbridges
Bassin de la Villette opens out — widest, flattest stretch
Parc de la Villette, or turn here for a 6 km round trip
Carry on up the Canal de l'Ourcq towards Pantin for 10 km and beyond

pairings.text: Ten Belles at the turnaround
Du Pain et des Idées, weekdays only

items.title: Hill Reps at Buttes-Chaumont
items.area: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
items.transit: M5 to Laumière, or run there along the canal
items.why: The only serious hill within reach, and the antidote to the canal being completely flat. A lap of the park is about 2 km with around 40 m of climb, and the staircases up to the temple are brutal enough that Paris running clubs use them for intervals. Three laps and you have done something. Sunday mornings it is full of people doing exactly this.

pairings.text: Brûlerie de Belleville after
Temple viewpoint for the cooldown

items.title: Long Run in the Bois de Vincennes
items.area: Bois de Vincennes
items.transit: M1 to Château de Vincennes
items.why: When the canal is not long enough. Nine hundred hectares of woodland with soft paths, two lakes and a signed circuit around Lac Daumesnil — you can put together anything from 5 km to a full marathon distance without repeating yourself. Softer underfoot than the city, which matters if you are building up mileage. The Bois de Boulogne is the western equivalent and hosts a free timed 5 km on Saturday mornings.

pairings.text: Parc Floral jazz on summer weekends
Château de Vincennes at the gate

items.title: The Viaduct Run
items.area: Coulée verte René-Dumont, Bastille to Vincennes
items.transit: M8 to Bastille, start behind the Opéra
items.why: Four and a half kilometres of garden along a disused railway viaduct, four metres above the traffic, with no road crossings for the first stretch. Narrow in places, so it is a morning run rather than a Sunday-afternoon one. Run it out to the Bois de Vincennes and back and you have a comfortable 12 km with something to look at the whole way.

pairings.text: Marché d’Aligre at the start
Blé Sucré madeleines, rue Antoine Vollon

items.title: Padel at Jules Ladoumègue
items.area: Stade Jules Ladoumègue, Porte de Pantin
items.priceNote: ~€5 per player per hour — municipal rate
items.transit: M5 to Porte de Pantin
items.why: Padel is the fastest-growing sport in France and the single easiest racket sport to be immediately bad at together — the walls keep the ball in play, so rallies happen from the first minute even if neither of you can play. Paris has eight clubs now, but this is the municipal one: about five euros each an hour instead of the thirty you would pay privately. Book through the city tennis site. Twenty minutes on line 5.

pairings.text: Parc de la Villette is next door
Coffee at Ourcq on the canal walk home

items.title: 4Padel — Outdoor Courts & Sports Bar
items.area: Eastern Paris — five outdoor courts plus three for pickleball
items.priceNote: ~€15–25 a discovery session · first one often free
items.transit: M9 or M1 east
items.why: The bigger, livelier option: five outdoor padel courts, three pickleball courts and a sports bar that stays open on summer evenings, so it works as a night out rather than a training session. Most Paris clubs run discovery sessions at €15–25 and many make the first one free. Use Playtomic to find two other players at your level if you want a proper doubles game.

pairings.text: The bar is on site — that is the point
Pickleball courts next to the padel ones

items.title: Pickleball — Paris’s First Dedicated Club
items.area: Paris Expo, Porte de Versailles · also Mathis (19th) and Croix-Nivert (15th)
items.transit: M12 to Porte de Versailles
items.why: You have almost certainly never played this, which is the reason to. Six indoor courts opened at Porte de Versailles at the end of 2025 — France’s first all-pickleball club — open seven days a week from 07:30 to 22:30. The rules take about four minutes to learn and the rallies are long, so it is unusually good for two people of different fitness. The municipal centre at Mathis in the 19th is closer if you just want to try it.

pairings.text: Parc Georges-Brassens and its Sunday book market
Rue du Commerce for lunch after

items.title: Paname Run Club — Mardisco & Coffee Runs
items.area: Meeting points move — central Paris
items.transit: Varies weekly — check Instagram
items.why: No-drop, free, and the best way to meet people in this city without going to a party. Two things to know: Tuesday is Mardisco, where a DJ plays as you run, and the weekend Coffee Run deliberately ends at a café. No-drop means nobody gets left behind, which is the only thing that matters if one of you is faster than the other.

pairings.text: The Coffee Run ends at one — that is the whole design
Weekend runs finish near a bakery more often than not

items.title: parkrun — Free Timed 5K, Saturdays
items.area: Bois de Boulogne and Parc Montsouris
items.transit: RER B to Cité Universitaire for Montsouris
items.why: Five kilometres, timed, free, every Saturday at nine, with a barcode you register once and keep for life. It is the least intimidating race in existence — people walk it — and it gives you a number to beat next week, which is a surprisingly effective way to make running a habit rather than a resolution. Montsouris is the prettier of the two.

pairings.text: Coffee at the Cité Universitaire gates
Parc Montsouris itself, once you have stopped wheezing

items.title: Kayak & Paddle on the Bassin de la Villette
items.area: Bassin de la Villette, quai de la Loire
items.transit: M5 to Stalingrad, or walk up the canal
items.why: You can hire a kayak or a paddleboard on the widest stretch of the canal, and spend an hour on water most people only ever walk beside. Seeing the Rotonde and the lift bridge from the surface rather than the towpath genuinely changes the neighbourhood. Cheap, easy, and nobody expects you to be able to do it.

pairings.text: Paris Plages is on the same quay in summer
Open-air cinema up at La Villette after

items.title: Free Outdoor Ping-Pong
items.area: Concrete tables in parks all over the city
items.priceNote: Free — bring bats and a ball
items.transit: Jardin Villemin has tables — M5 to Jacques Bonsergent
items.why: There are permanent concrete tables in parks across Paris, including Jardin Villemin beside the canal, and they cost nothing. Keep two bats and a ball by the door and this becomes the easiest twenty minutes of sport in your week — the sort of thing you actually do, as opposed to the gym membership you mean to use.

pairings.text: Jardin Villemin is the table nearest you
Canal for a drink after, two minutes away

items.title: Vélib’ Along the Car-Free Seine
items.area: Voie Georges-Pompidou, right bank
items.transit: Any Vélib’ station — join the river at Bastille or the Louvre
items.why: The lower right bank of the Seine has been closed to cars since 2016 and most people still think of it as a road. Take a Vélib’ down to the water and ride it end to end — Bastille to the Louvre and back is about an hour, entirely traffic-free, past the Île Saint-Louis at water level. Best at eight in the morning or an hour before sunset.

pairings.text: Berthillon on Île Saint-Louis, mid-ride
Square du Vert-Galant at the island’s tip for sunset

items.title: Skate & Roll at République
items.area: Place de la République
items.transit: M3/M5/M8/M9/M11 to République
items.why: The pedestrianised half of République has been an informal skate spot for years — beginners at one end, people doing things that look impossible at the other, most evenings. Even if you never step on a board it is a good place to sit with a drink and watch. Paris also has a Friday-night mass roller skate that takes over the streets; look up Pari Roller if that appeals.

pairings.text: Le Syndicat is eight minutes away
Late pizza around rue du Faubourg-du-Temple

items.title: Bouldering in the Fontainebleau Forest
items.area: Forest of Fontainebleau — Bas Cuvier, Trois Pignons
items.transit: Gare de Lyon to Fontainebleau-Avon, then bus
items.why: One of the birthplaces of the sport, an hour from Paris: thousands of sandstone boulders in a forest, with colour-coded circuits so you can follow a graded line rather than guess. The easiest circuits are genuinely doable by beginners. Autumn is the season — cold rock, dry sand, no crowds. Pair it with the château if you want the day to have two halves.

pairings.text: Château de Fontainebleau in the morning
The forest walks if arms give out first

items.title: Free Outdoor Yoga & Park Fitness
items.area: Parks across the city — Buttes-Chaumont, Villette, Bercy
items.transit: M5 to Laumière for Buttes-Chaumont
items.why: The city runs free open-air sport sessions in the parks from spring to autumn — yoga, stretching, circuit training, most of them turn-up-and-join. There are also permanent outdoor fitness installations dotted through the bigger parks. It is the cheapest possible way to find out whether you actually like something before paying a studio forty euros to discover you do not.

pairings.text: Rosa Bonheur in the park for a drink after
Bakeries on rue de Meaux on the way home

items.title: Winter Ice Rinks
items.area: Pop-up rinks — Hôtel de Ville and around the city
items.transit: M1 to Hôtel de Ville
items.why: From December the city puts temporary rinks up in front of the Hôtel de Ville and elsewhere, and they are cheap, chaotic and much more fun than they sound. Worth putting in the calendar now, because they appear and vanish within about six weeks and it is easy to look up in February and realise you missed it.

pairings.text: Hot chocolate at Angelina or a Marais café
Christmas lights on rue de Rivoli
